idiom_name: nested def capturing the enclosing method's parameters and locals (vars boxed)
implementation_notes: Scala nests method definitions: a def inside another def is visible only there and can use the enclosing method's parameters directly, which removes the parameter plumbing that motivated the pattern (Tour of Scala). Nested defs and function literals capture the variables themselves, so mutations are visible in both directions; when a captured var is written the compiler boxes it into a reference object, and returning the function turns the environment into an anonymous class instance. Prefer a local class or a private method on the host when the algorithm must be a reusable, testable type; use nested defs for the single-use computation.
pitfalls: A captured var that is written is heap-boxed, so nested defs over mutable state allocate in tight loops; prefer threading values or a local class with fields.
Nested defs are not first-class values without eta-expansion (sum _ in Scala 2) and cannot be tested directly from outside the enclosing method.
Deeply nested defs hide the algorithm's shape; once the capture list grows, a local class documents the shared state better.
